# Tries, palindrome checks, and suffix automata

A trie stores strings by shared prefixes and makes prefix counting a graph
walk. Palindrome queries can be checked with hashes in large settings; the
local exercise first uses direct mirrored comparisons so the equality condition
is completely visible before introducing hashes. A suffix automaton compactly represents all substrings: each state contributes
`len[state] - len[link[state]]` new substrings.

## Trie prefix counting

A trie is a rooted tree where each edge is labeled by a character. A word is a
root-to-node path. To answer "how many dictionary words have prefix `p`", store
`cnt[v]`: how many inserted words pass through node `v`.

Insertion:

```text
node = root
for c in word:
    create edge c if missing
    node = child[node][c]
    cnt[node] += 1
```

Query:

```text
walk the prefix
if an edge is missing: answer 0
else answer cnt[last_node]
```

The invariant is simple: after all insertions, `cnt[v]` equals the number of
words whose path includes `v`.

## Palindrome substring queries

For a substring `s[l..r]`, the direct check compares mirrored characters:

```text
s[l] with s[r]
s[l+1] with s[r-1]
...
```

This is `O(length)` and is useful for teaching correctness. In larger
contests, use rolling hashes:

```text
hash_forward(l,r) == hash_reverse(n-1-r, n-1-l)
```

Hashing is fast but probabilistic unless you use deterministic structures such
as suffix arrays or palindromic trees. When constraints permit direct checking,
the exact method is safer.

## Distinct substrings and suffix automaton idea

A suffix automaton is a compressed DFA containing all substrings of a string.
For each state `v`:

- `len[v]` is the maximum length of a substring represented by `v`;
- `link[v]` points to the state representing the longest proper suffix class.

The number of new substrings contributed by `v` is:

```text
len[v] - len[link[v]]
```

Summing this over all states except the initial state gives the number of
distinct non-empty substrings.

For a pedagogical local problem, suffix-array or direct-set solutions may be
used at small limits, but the formula above is the red-level invariant you
should know.

## Recognition table

| Problem form | Tool |
|---|---|
| dictionary prefixes | trie |
| repeated substring equality | rolling hash or suffix array |
| palindrome range query | forward/reverse hash, Manacher, eertree |
| count distinct substrings | suffix automaton or suffix array |

## Distinct substrings by hand

For `s = aba`, the distinct non-empty substrings are:

```text
a, b, ab, ba, aba
```

There are `5`. A suffix automaton reaches the same count by summing:

```text
len[state] - len[link[state]]
```

over states. The formula counts how many new substring lengths become possible
when that state is created. The direct enumeration is fine for tiny strings;
the automaton is what makes the same idea linear for large strings.

## Trie example

Insert:

```text
app, apple, ape
```

The node for prefix `ap` has counter `3`. The node for `app` has counter `2`.
The node for `apple` has counter `1`. A missing edge answers `0` immediately.

## Hash versus automaton versus trie

These tools solve different string questions:

```text
trie: many dictionary prefixes
hash: fast equality checks between substrings
suffix automaton: all substrings of one string
```

Do not use a suffix automaton for prefix dictionary queries; it is the wrong
shape. Do not use a trie to compare arbitrary substrings inside one long text.
Choosing the representation is the main skill in this section.

## Practice drill

For any string problem, write which object is being queried:

```text
prefix of dictionary word
substring of one text
suffix of one text
palindrome centered somewhere
set of all substrings
```

Then choose the representation. A trie is a prefix tree. A hash is a comparison
tool. A suffix automaton is a compressed representation of all substrings. This
one sentence prevents many overcomplicated solutions.

# Exercises

- A. Trie Prefix Count: Given dictionary words and prefix queries, count words having each prefix.
- B. Palindrome Queries: For each substring query, print whether the substring is a palindrome.
- C. Distinct Substrings: Print the number of distinct non-empty substrings of a string.
